speechtext: I ask the hon. member to drop the third .part of this question. There can be only one reason for that question, namely to draw some inference that these men are not doing their duty. The Department of National Defence and the officers responsible take full responsibility for these men being at their posts. We are quite willing to give the number of men and to take whatever responsibility or criticism there may be for having men of that age at headquarters; but to give the names of these men is quite a different thing. It seems to me that in fairness to them one would have to give opposite their names the reasons why they are in these posts; therefore I will ask my hon. friend to drop the question. This station farm has been organized on a six year rotation basis, aiming to give community leadership by contributing to a better understanding of the best cultural methods, fertilizer practices and cropping procedures to associate with the efficient utilization of irrigation water. speechtext:
Will the Minister of Labour make a statement
Labour Conditions

to the house regarding the proposed lay-off of men. at the John Inglis Toronto plant? According to my information from the trade union officials it involves about three thousand men.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY-GENERAL PURCHASING BRANCH  CEILING PRICES
subtopic: JOHN INGLIS PLANT, TORONTO-CHANGES IN PRODUCTION REQUIREMENTS AND SCHEDULES -TRANSFER OF LABOUR
speechtext:
I know the circumstances.
There have been, two or three suggestions in the house with regard to lay-offs in the John Inglis plant, but so far as I am aware no man has been laid off there up to this date. So far as I know, there is no immediate proposal to lay off men. However, we are facing a situation which all hon. members should understand. The war has reached the point where we have' now filled the initial requirements for certain types of equipment. We have provided all the initial requirements of the troops plus the required number of spares. Future requirements will depend on usage. Once capital requirements are filled, usage requirements are smaller. We are now revising our programme with that in mind. There are other phases that must be considered, one being that the war has passed from the defensive to the offensive stage, so that certain defensive weapons such as anti-aircraft guns are not now needed to the extent that they were some time ago. We are also directing the course of the war instead of permitting the enemy to do so. It is no longer necessary to put supplies of arms into countries that are likely to be attacked. We can now concentrate our supplies as the offensive strategy of Britain and her allies directs. AH these considerations have caused changes in the production requirements and production schedules of the allied countries. We are revising our scheduler Items that are likely to be affected are all types of army guns, from small arms up to the largest calibre guns, including anti-aircraft guns and many types of artillery ammunition. I think that is the general range of items that will be curtailed. In the course of time the schedule calls for making considerably fewer Bren guns than are being made now, and there will be a reduction accordingly, in the staff of the Bren gun plant, arising from the fact that the present rate of output of guns from that plant is no longer required.
As regards closing, there is nothing definite about it. When the men will be laid off is a matter that is indefinite, but I would point out that there is a very serious over-all shortage of man-power in war industry to-day. I know of very few plants that have the number of men required to permit them to. obtain the desired output. What will happen will

be a transfer of labour from plants making less urgently required equipment to plants making equipment for which there is greater urgency. I sincerely hope that I shall not have to answer a question in the house every time men are changed from one plant to another. I am stating the whole programme to-day and there is nothing more that I can add to it. Transfers will be effected by selective service and they will be rather frequent over the course of the next three or four months.

At six o'clock last evening I had been commenting upon the committee which is to be appointed to carry on the activities envisaged by this bill, and I said I thought the committee, which is being

selected from the members of the cabinet, was being chosen wisely, since the members of the committee would be directly responsible to the cabinet and to the House of Commons. I had also expressed approval of the number of members of the committee. I was going on to point out that when the federal Department of Finance had in it men who were realistic in their outlook with respect to financial matters, then the standard of living in Canada could be raised through the activities of this committee to a level which would conform to the ability of the country to produce goods and services. I had pointed out that this committee will have very important functions to perform. First of all its work will have to do with the war; then it will have to do with the reconstruction period before the treaty of peace is signed, and later there will be definite and responsible work for this committee to do during the time of peace which will follow the signing of the treaty.
It may be argued that the life of this bill is only one year, but as I see it this is only the first of a long series of acts which will be based on the principle of lease-lend. When the time comes for the world to settle down to peaceful pursuits, we shall find it necessary to carry on mutual aid operations for the benefit of countries whose resources are not adequate to support the standard of life which ought to obtain there, considering the period of the world's history in which we shall be living. It wiH >be necessary, therefore, for us to have boards like this and acts like this to enable Canada to contribute her portion of the goods which must be contributed by the nations possessing rich resources, in order that the nations less abundantly equipped may be able to enjoy a fair standard of living.

just a word with reference to the amendment that has been proposed. I agree with some of the other hon. members who have spoken that the committee which is to be set up may have an important influence upon the trade policies of Canada following the war. I am. satisfied that the United States, in. regard to its lease-lend bill, certainly has an eye to its future trade policies. In my opinion many of our past difficulties with respect to agriculture have arisen from the fact that we have had one minister responsible for production and another minister responsible for marketing, an arrangement in which I have never been able to see any sound economy. In my view the Minister of Trade and Commerce, by virtue of his office, should be, next to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the most important member of this committee. Yesterday I asked a question concerning an agricultural commodity delivered to Britain under the aid bill of last year. Four of the five proposed members of this committee were present, yet I was unable to obtain an answer to my question. Certainly I think the Minister of Agriculture should be a member of this committee, as it is proposed he shall be, but I believe it most important not only to agriculture but to the future well-being of the w'hole country that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should be a member also, because no matter what our occupation may be our future welfare depends upon the trade of the country. This bill is to deal with a war condition, but you cannot dissociate its operation from matters of trade which will have a distinct bearing on the future of this country. Therefore I hope the minister may see fit to accept this amendment and include the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this committee.

speechtext:
The first thing to keep in
mind in discussing this amendment, and I know every hon. member does keep it in mind, is that we must not have any regard whatever to personalities. So far as my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is concerned, everyone has high regard for him.; his judgment is of the best, and
he would be an addition to any committee or deliberative body. But the question whether or not the Minister of Trade andi Commerce should be a member of the Mutual Aid board must be determined upon entirely different considerations. I should tell the committee that we set out to keep this committee or board just as small as possible. If we couldihave had a board of three or of two members it would have been desirable, other things being equal, because, generally speaking, the smaller the boards, the more expeditious are their proceedings. But it seemed to be impossible to . escape the appointment of five members of the cabinet, and there are- compelling, and strong reasons for the selection of all those selected. The Minister of Munitions and Supply would of course have to be on the board. He would be the proper minister to act as chairman. He is in charge of the procurement of munitions, and their production in this country, which are the foundation of the greater part of the operations of the board. But there is another important group of products in Canada, namely the products of the farm. The procurement agency for agricultural products is the Department of Agriculture, headed by the Minister of Agriculture. It was thought necessary that he be made a member of the board. - Between them, those two members cover nearly the whole field-not the whole of it, of course, but nearly the whole of it. Their departments cover the range of products which will be supplied, to our allies. It was necessary to have the defence departments represented. There were excellent reasons for appointing all three defence ministers to the board, because each has a vital interest in the allocation of munitions as between the requirements of our own services and those of the services of other countries. It was finally decided, however, in the interests of keeping the board small, that the Minister of National Defence should serve as the representative of the three defence departments, although the other two defence departments _ have a vital interest in the allocation of munitions and supplies.
I believe the reason for having the Minister of Finance on the board is a compelling one. Finance must be represented, not only for the reason mentioned by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, the extent and importance of the financial expenditures involved, but because a shortage of Canadian dollars is an important criterion for a country receiving assistance under the act. The Department of Finance is the only one which can supply information and advice on that point. It must say whether goods should be charged
Mutual Aid Bill

to the war appropriation, or to the Mutual Aid appropriation. That is distinctly a financial problem and indeed a difficult one. Therefore it was necessary to have the Minister of Finance on the board. The Minister of Justice was appointed to the board because arrangements will be made by exchanges of notes, agreements and the like, in respect of the supply of these goods, with various governments. In my opinion no one in the government or outside of it would be more competent to advise and guide on matters of the kind than would the Minister of Justice.

The other day the minister saw fit to suggest that it was a concoction when I pointed that out as a power which he could use. From the minister's own lips there now comes an admission of the possibility of what I suggested the other day.
I say to the minister that we are one hundred per cent for legislation such as this; we are for any legislation which will assist the united nations, which will assist in the common defence against the common enemy, but we in this parliament have the right to know whether or not this legislation is designed for one purpose only, that of providing common aid for the common defence of the united nations. The minister should bring in an amendment stating that this legislation will not be used as a means of securing concessions in connection with trade or otherwise. Let us be clear on that. Let us tell the other united nations that Canada by this contribution, if you will, is coming to their assistance without regard to the possibility of what considerations may be secured after the war.
That was the essence of what I said the other day, and at that time the minister suggested that I was building up brick by brick an imaginary edifice. I built up that edifice on the basis of the legislation that he brought before parliament. I did that only because I was aware of the fact that in the United States provision was made for reciprocal arrangements. But he gave us his assurance that that was not the purpose here, that he did not have it in mind. I pointed out the possibilities, and to-day he says, that under this legislation these possibilities remain. He mentioned the agreements and the notes which had passed between Canada and the United States in November last. I have them before me. There is no suggestion here that the dealings between Canada and the United States under lend-lease are to be on a cash basis. If I read them aright, these notes are all based on the one fact. I have here the letter from the Canadian legation in Washington to the Secretary of State of the United States of America, dated November 30 last, wherein the following appears:
Our two governments are prepared to cooperate in formulating a programme of agreed action, open to participation by all other countries of like mind, directed to the expansion, by appropriate international and domestic measures, of production, employment, and th.e exchange and consumption of goods, which are the material foundations of the liberty and welfare of all peoples; to the elimination of all forms of discriminatory treatment in international commerce. . . .
We have the right to ask what conversations have taken place between. Canada and the United States with respect to the matter of lend-lease, and what conversations have taken place between Canada and any other of the united nations. When I asked yesterday

Mutual Aid Bill

whether agricultural products were to be disposed of under the terms of this legislation, the. minister said that we may do so but it was felt that we would be selling most of our agricultural products. We have the right to be assured, the Canadian farmer has the right to be assured, that when this bill becomes law we shall be ready to turn over to any of the united nations which may be in need of Canadian farm products, the surplus wheat we have to-day, and that a reasonable price will be paid to the farmer. We are prepared to advance a billion dollars to provide war munitions and supplies, including wheat. Here is an opportunity under this legislation to give the farmer a fair and reasonable price, a parity price for his wheat. It could be purchased by the Canadian government and turned over to the needy nations. Here is the question I asked yesterday and the minister's reply as reported on page 2615 of Hansard,-.

We are going to turn over munitions; we may turn over various other supplies, and we have the power to turn over agricultural products. However, the inference is that it is not intended to do so.

I was surprised to note that even in the government press there was no hallelujah chorus about the set-up in this particular bill. There was hardly any government paper that supported this section 3, and one government evening paper last night in the edition I read, carried no report of this measure. There was a complete absence of the hosanna and hip-hurrah chorus of the government press which generally accompanies a lot of these measures, and praise of the controls and subcontrols. Are we to get value for this money? The government has had some experience since this war started in connection with these matters, but what did we find yesterday? The whole civil service was ignored. It was announced yesterday in the government morning papers that a Mr. Fraser, who was assistant to E. P. Taylor at Washington, is to become head of the department, over the heads of the whole civil service, of all these experienced people, at probably may^be three or four times their salary. I can tell the minister that the country is much disatisfied with this state of things. When the set-up goes into effect what shall we have? A secret star chamber-that is what it is- the governor in council, passing on these applications from what they call the "allies". New allies can be added overnight by a stroke of the pen perhaps some of them will be those who so far sat on the fence, as I remarked the other day.
The point is that in consenting to this political set-up in section 3 parliament is losing forever all control over this lease-lend bill. No longer is information to be handed over to the daily press. Some of the government and other papers are silent on this set-up of a committee of the cabinet in charge of this. It seems to me that we might as well be meeting in secret for all the information we can get on what goes on down here from most of the press. Since the last war we have observed the commercializing of the press. This has been especially evident in the case of some large dailies, with millions of subscribers, as in London and New York, and1 which are not giving the people the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth about this war. They sit on the fence and will not take sides on some contentious matters to keep popular with their readers. We shall never get our proceedings reported so long as the government continues to ignore the press the way it has been doing. I contend it is the press which should do this publicity work, this educating the people as to what goes on here in parliament, although I do not blame them, in view of

Mutual Aid Bill
the way they are used, for not doing it; they are not entirely to blame for not publishing the proceedings of parliament better. We ourselves are mostly responsible for the people being blindfolded and deprived of information as to what goes on here, because we allow control by bodies like the governor in council and information boards and amateur censors; we acquiesce in the taking away of rights and privileges and functions which have been ours from time immemorial. Virtually we might as well go home and1, as one hon. gentleman said on Monday, put a padlock on the door. I cannot reproduce the Parisian accent of my hon. friend from Vancouver East on how to pronounce Temis-couata* but in this matter the hon. member for Temiscouata, with the word "padlock", hit the nail on the head. The people will be much dissatisfied about the arrangements for the distribution of lease-lend funds under this particular bill, whether for war purposes or for the rebuilding of Europe after the war. Control is vested in an executive committee of the cabinet-for that is all they are- consisting of five ministers. All of them are good men, doing good work. I did not object yesterday to inclusion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce; far from it; but I am opposed to any ministers being oil a committee of this kind. I am in favour of an administrator being appointed and made responsible to this parliament.
I believe the people will have little confidence in the distribution of this fund, whether from a commercial, a military, or a humanitarian aspect under this set-up. We all know that certain allies are doing the work ana certain other- are getting the credit. We know that information is given out in the form of canned interviews by the information bureau. We know that this is what has happened regarding this very bill, even before it is passed by the House of Commons. If such canned information is to be distributed as it is done now by the administration, and other departments are to be ignored, it will not be possible to find out the facts about the distribution of this Mutual Aid fund. We. shall never have a proper system so long as an outsider is brought in to operate over the heads of trained civil servants of the army, the navy and the air force, men who have worked all their lives for this country, who constitute some of the ablest administrators we have, and who have carried on conscientiously and faithfully on small salaries, struggling to pay their income tax. I have read in Houston's, annual about the corporations with which
72537-167*
some of these control men the government brought in are connected. Some of these corporations have contracts with the government, although some of their executive directors are serving as controllers and under the government, and they have more influence with the cabinet than not a few hon, members.
I am unable to understand what reason there can be for dividing the departmental controls of his majesty's forces. The young minister who represented Kingston City in 1940 and 1941 had under his control the whole of the three departments now concerned with the army, the navy and the air force. With all this multiplication of machinery in a population of ten millions, what is the result? Overtaxation and waste. Widespread waste of money, duplication, such as one sees around Ottawa, where you have a building the size of Eaton's to house one department, and then another department comes along and wants accommodation of equal size, spending money like water. I have never seen extravagance to approach it. They are sending opera company shows all over the country. The army wants a show, the navy wants a show, and then the air force want another.

speechtext:
It was said by a distinguished French soldier concerning the charge of the Light Brigade, "C'est magnifique, mais ce n'est pas la guerre." It is magnificent, but it is not war. That remark can well be applied to this magnificent ceremonial performance and special trains and special actors and actresses, and to the whole of our present methods of doing business. These information bureaus and picture bureaus and liaison press officers, and information they get out are nothing very largely but a waste of money. The people of this country are very much aroused about these things.
Who is going to audit the accounts under this lease-lend bill? Is it the auditor general? No. According to the audit act, which I quoted last session, the auditor general cannot audit one cent of the five billion dollars or of the three and a half billion dollars allotted for the -war. A short time ago there was appointed a comptroller of the treasury. By virtue of the appropriation bill of five or six clauses which the minister introduced, as long as any item of this three and a half billion dollars expenditure comes under one of these sections the comptroller of the treasury puts the stamp on it. This house should be careful about giving away its privileges under section 3 of this bill, then, because it will not get them
Mutual Aid Bill

back after the war is over. There is supposed to be a check by the committee of the house on war expenditures. Well, what check have they got? All they do, as far as I can see,-and their reports have never been discussed in the house-is, when the session is over, visit some plants and make a Cook's tour through Canada. I am glad they do; they are entitled to the trip and to proper privileges, and I appreciate the good work they are doing. But so far as any control of the treasury or its expenditures is concerned, there is none and there will be none under section 3 of this lease-lend bill either.
As I said yesterday, there will be sure to be politics in the administration of this fund; there is no doubt about that. In my opinion there was a great deal of wisdom and truth in what was said on this matter yesterday by my hon. and learned friend from York-Sunbury, but his criticisms elicited no reply whatever from the government. The procedure in these big spending boards in wartime, is to bring in some outsider who has always been a good Liberal. I have no objection to the Liberals; they are a good party and they have done a good deal of useful work for Canada and in this war; but I say to them, you should not pass over the trained men. of the civil service for unknown outsiders. Where could you go outside into the country or to the United States and get an official like the Clerk of the House of Commons, who handles the work with so much knowledge, experience and ability? He is only one of a splendid type of civil servants and officials who have given their lives and their services night and day to this country; there are deputy ministers and others of great competence in every department, but their wisdom and experience are ignored, they are passed over and other men brought in.
What will Mr. Fraser do if he comes in as head of a department? He will probably engage two or three members of the civil service, presumably not top-notchers but third-class clerks, and then some sisters and cousins and aunts of the controllers may be brought in to assist in the administration, and by and by he will build up a duplicate spending department of great magnitude with another regiment of. officials. Take the head of the wartime prices and trade board as an illustration of the extent to which we have given away our privileges to controls. Consider the power that has been placed in the hands of Donald Gordon. He is a czar. Well, if they have made a czar of Donald Gordon why have not the government appointed somebody, an inside civil servant preferably, to handle in an independent way the administration of this lease-lend bill?

Time is the essence of the contract in this lease-lend administration, but I predict that the people of Europe will be starving for months before they get any help, if we are to have this antiquated system carried on by a committee of the cabinet.
I do not know in how many committees members of the cabinet are engaged. I saw a book the other day that gave a list showing that some of them were serving on fifteen or twenty subcommittees. Political ignorance and apathy are the two greatest enemies of the democracies, and by the same token they are the best friends of the axis powers. Why not give the public the real picture. It is the function of a democratic government to support a democratic press, so that the taxpayers may obtain, through the medium of that press, information in regard to the expenditure of public moneys such as is contemplated here. After all, the taxpayer is the man who is going to foot the bill; the cost will not be paid by a committee of the cabinet or by this committee. It is the taxpayers of Canada who will have to pay it. They will get it in their income tax and in other ways. I submit therefore that it is the duty of the government to make it possible for the people to get all the information they can. I do not blame the press for not publicizing the matter when the government has shown such a lack of confidence in the press of Canada by appointing an information bureau to discharge the functions that should properly be discharged by our newspapers. It should be the function of the press to obtain the necessary information from the government in regard to bill 76 and to give a real picture of what is going on, not only in our domestic affairs but in regard to foreign questions as well, and to stimulate interest in public affairs. For that reason I am opposed to the information bureau. I have objected to it because I do not believe that it is in the interests of the country to appoint a bureau to explain the bill and to give interviews in regard to section 3 and other provisions of the bill.
The government. I repeat, has shown lack of confidence in the ability of our press to fulfil its proper function, which should be to supply the public with information to which the taxpayers are entitled. We as a House of Commons should protect the taxpayers and see that the people are kept in touch with what is going on. And there is only one agency through which information can reach the people. That is the press. When you next come to censorship which will [DOT]further keep this house from the facts and the people also, I would ask the government, how

Mutual Aid Bill
will the House of Commons find out what is going on? How shall we know what this committee of the cabinet are doing in handling this business? The censor will come along and we shall find that not even members of the House of Commons will get any information, because it is not in the public interest. It is provided that a report shall be presented to parliament, and of course the money will have to be provided. In my opinion this policy of carrying on is simply a relic of other days. This system would not have been tolerated in the other war; and as far as lease-lend is concerned, if we are to be running to Washington all the time and copying everything they do, and if we are to follow the star chamber method of appointing committees like this to handle matters of this sort, taking it out of the hands of the people's representatives, then we shall certainly become the Washington of the north.
At the start of this session everybody got the idea that the war with Germany would be over in a very short time,- and a red herring w-as drawn across the trail, giving social security the place of the war, although the war was primary and we were in it. Steps were taken early here this year, forgetting largely the war accordingly, to investigate the new order and to make provision for the new paradise that we were going to have, a land of milk and honey, as Ramsay MacDonald once said. We started the session on January 27, and for the first two weeks we heard nothing about committees and then the committees were appointed. The government would not allow a committee of the cabinet to run the Canadian National railways, which is a public utility, and I suggest that if an outside commission can handle the national railways, the radio, the control boards and several other services of that sort, there is no reason why the government should not appoint a body to handle these matters.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health is a hard-working man, and he has done a good deal of work in connection with pensions and health. It was said humorously by a lady sweeping the floors here that by chipping in fifty cents we would all get all the food and clothing we wanted forever, and that the fifty cents would include all the medicine you wanted. But you would only get a bottle of that kind of medicine every week-end, not one every day. Well, we have dropped the committee system like hot cakes in this bill for a subcommittee of the cabinet called the privy council. They do not wear the privy council uniforms when they sit around the lease-lend table to get
information. The ministers who have been named are busy gentlemen and I sympathize with them for the hard work they are doing.
I do not know anyone who would want to substitute for the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Munitions and Supply or the Minister of National Defence. The hon. member for Temiscouata said that he would not want to be nominated to be one of these secretaries to ministers and I do not blame him, because one would have to be up all day long and at night too to work like the ministry on this bill.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I submit that the government is making a fatal mistake in the conduct of the war. Party politics will be rampant. Everywhere you go they will be talking about the lease-lend bill on every political platform and the poor suffering people in Europe will be left starving, without munitions or food supplies, while these committees are meeting and selecting what countries and allies to aid.

And I am wondering whether one of the reasons for this bill is not to help take up the slack in a period of unemployment facing this country during the transition.
The trouble with our war planning is that in 1940 after Dunkirk we became panicky and rushed into everything. Perhaps I have some responsibility for that, and if so I am quite willing to assume my share, because I urged upon this government that they do everything possible to make and ship things to aid the distress of the one power that was withstanding the hun. But we never had any coordinated plan of production from that day until recently when certain boards were set up. The result is that we have gone along and produced, and to-day there is no longer any necessity for some of this production. I am told that of certain types of machine guns they have so many they do not know what to do with them. We have one contract for Lewis guns, an initial order of one thousand, and they do not want them. They have not been produced yet. As a matter of fact they have so many they do not know what to do with them. The Minister of Munitions and Suppfy may deny that there is an immediate prospect of a lay-off at the John Inglis plant. Why? Because they have a great surplus of Bren guns in

I am not going to object very much to that; I just want the information. Is it so, or is it not so? I realize that there will be grave difficulty in this country if there is any period of unemployment in the congested industrial centres.
I return, however, to the thesis that a substantial portion of this grant should be used for food. I think perhaps parliament could toss it back, but all the Americans are asking for is contained in article VII of the lend-lease agreement. They say:
In the final determination of the benefits-
They were talking about benefits in their legislation.
-to be provided to the United States of America by the government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics-
This was the agreement with Russia.
-in return for aid furnished under the act of congress of March 11, 1941, the terms and conditions thereof shall be such as not to burden commerce between the two countries, but to promote mutually advantageous economic relations between them and the betterment of world wide economic relations. To that end, they shall include provision for agreed action by the United States of America and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, open to participation by all other countries of like mind, directed to the expansion, by appropriate international and domestic measures, of production, employment, and the exchange and consumption of goods, -which are the material foundations of the liberty and welfare of all peoples; to the elimination of all forms of discriminatory-treatment in international commerce, and to the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers; and, in general, to the attainment of all the economic objectives set forth in the joint declaration made on August 12, 1941, by the President of the United States of America and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, the basic principles of which were adhered to by the government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics on September 24, 1941.
At- an early convenient date, conversations shall be begun between the two governments with a view to determining, in the light of governing economic conditions, the best means of attaining the above stated objectives by their own agreed action and of seeking the agreed action of other like-minded governments.
In the exchange of notes we subscribed to these principles. It might very well be that we would ask some country to which we supplied goods to subscribe to a similar set of principles. But the minister did not think there was any association between the two. As to being a concession-hunter- well, if seeking parity within Canada means that I am a concession hunter, then I am guilty. I have always argued there should be some parity in connection with services rendered and goods produced in connection with the war effort. I am concerned in the transactions connected with the war, and our war effort, and I do say that the agricultural population of this country are entitled to the same consideration as are the workers in industry or those engaged in any other vocations. They are entitled to the same consideration from this government.	These
services should be divided up within the country, and under this Mutual Aid bill agricultural ' products are entitled to just consideration.
The minister raised the question with the hon. member for Lake Centre as to what difference prices can make to the agricultural producer.	The more goods those people
deliver, the more it will mean to agricultural income in Canada and to the individual farmer and producer. As was pointed out the other day by the hon. member for Lake Centre, we have every faith in the sincerity of the Minister of Finance. As I have said before, it is my belief that he is a conscientious minister. But we are delegating a tremendous authority to this board. I cannot make myself believe that some of the matters taken before the board under this measure will not in some degree affect the future policy of this country. I think all are agreed that the greatest essential in the post-war period will be foodstuffs, and chiefly the production of agricultural products to feed the peoples of those overrun nations. I think we have reached the point where we are satisfied we are going to win the war. Whether by design or not, in some degree we are establishing principles and policies for the future.
In my opinion we should give this matter serious consideration, because whether we conscientiously believe we are doing so or not, the fact is that we are developing and in some measure setting up a trade policy for the future.

Hon. members have talked about wheat. I just wish to have clear what they would like to have. They want a lot of this money devoted to the giving away of wheat, as I understand it. To begin with, it is not possible to ship wheat to countries which do not need it, and countries which do need if are getting it to the extent that shipping
Mutual Aid Bill

facilities are available. We sent it to Russia, to Greece and to Great Britain. No country will take wheat that has no ships to carry it, unless wheat is required. It is unreasonable to take the position that we should send wheat and use up critical shipping space-send wheat to countries which do not need it, to get rid of the surplus so as to enhance the price to the farmers of this country. That is an unreasonable position.

maintopic: MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY-GENERAL PURCHASING BRANCH  CEILING PRICES
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF SI,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OF WAR SUPPLIES
speechtext:
With regard to wheat, I think the minister is quite right when he says we have not the shipping facilities available to ship surplus wheat. I should like to point out, however, that the world is going to need far more wheat than we can grow in the years immediately following the war. We will' need this wheat now on our farms. There are over a billion bushels of grain to-day in storage on farms in western Canada, and farmers are suffering seriously because they cannot sell it. Here is an opportunity for the government to make advances to the fanner for the grain stored on the farm. The farmers could be given initial payments for all grain properly stored, and it could be left there for them to hold, the government paying the balance when the wheat can be shipped. An immediate initial payment could be made. If we leave this situation as it is and the time comes when we need far more wheat than we have for delivery, we are placing the whole burden on the backs of the farmers.
As I said in respect of a similar measure last year, the board is going to be allowed to purchase this grain, or any other commodity, or make it available in any way the board wishes. So far they have been purchasing grain through the wheat board. The farmer is not guaranteed a parity price. Here is an opportunity for the government to see that he gets a parity price for his commodity. He is about the only person producing commodities for shipment who is not receiving the cost of production. He must carry the burden of storing the wheat until it is required. Here is an opportunity to give him justice.
In paying his taxes, the farmer makes his contribution to Canada's gift to other nations, when she buys war materials, war supplies, tanks, guns and things of that kind. The producer of those manufactured articles is guaranteed his price, but the farmer, when making his contribution of wheat, is not guaranteed even his cost of production. Purchases are always made through the processors or handlers of his products, and those processors are guaranteed their price. The pork processor gets the price he wants.
The farmer is to-day carrying the burden of storing the food which will be required. This measure affords an opportunity to the 
government to relieve the situation, and do something to help the farmer. I made a similar statement in respect of last year's bill, and I make it again to-day.

speechtext: I realize that the Minister of Finance was being facetious when he described some of us as concession hunters. If he will read what I said yesterday I think he will see that I did not say anything to indicate that Canada should try to drive a hard bargain with any of the united nations. That thought was not in my mind at all. What I had in mind was that it would increase the efficiency of the board if the Minister of Trade and Commerce were made a member. After all, his department should know more about trade and commerce than any other department, since that has been their business for many decades. They have had trade commissioners in many countries and if he were made a member of this board that would increase its efficiency in handling the products that are to be sent abroad and perhaps would bring about a wiser distribution. speechtext: I have another amendment to move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski. It is a simple thing. We have heard that the ministers were so busy that, as the Prime Minister told us, it was hard for them to meet hon. members even in the corridors and elsewhere. It was said when the parliamentary secretaries were appointed that it would be cruel to impose on ministers the task of attending sittings of boards like this. It is really cruel, when the ministers are doing so much work, and are absorbed in their own departments, especially those ministers who have to be on boards, and the only thing to do is to suggest that this board should be composed of parliamentary secretaries. These hon. members, as it has been said, have the confidence of the ministers; high tribute has been paid to all of them; but they have not been given an opportunity to show what they can do. Yes, I did', the same as
my hon. friend; but since neither of us has succeeded we must accept the state of things as it exists. It is the policy of the accomplished fact. My hon. friend has done his duty; I have done mine. Most unfortunately, we did not succeed in opening the eyes of those who were in the majority; and I accept on this question the decision of the majority because we cannot reverse it. But do you not think this amendment is the more timely because the committee has just turned down an amendment to add another minister? I wonder who drafted this bill; but the committee does not seem inclined to have a board like this composed of ministers.
With regard to what is at the base of this bill, aid to those who need it, nobody has any objection to it, upon two conditions. The first one is that satisfactory account is rendered of what has been done in the past; the second is, reasonable assurance that this bill will help those who really need help and will not serve only to increase the wealth of the mandarins. What I mean by mandarins is, speaking of Chinese politics, those who take personal advantage of what is supposed to be given to the needy. They are what we call in this country "toll-gates". In China the practice is quite common. Since we have started a new policy of our own, I wonder if it is not the experience of the bank for international settlements, which has been reported to us by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay, which has induced the government to deal direct with the united nations without passing through the canal of last year. What was revealed to us by our colleague the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay was far from being edifying, but he quoted from official papers, from the Westminster Debates. I am a little concerned about the clutching hands of high finance in dealing with very large sums of money. I do not know of any other minister, not even the Minister of Finance, who has the president of a bank as his adviser. The Minister of Finance is supposed to get advice from the presidents of all the banks, and he has not one president attached to him as his own adviser. I find it tough, and I think the Minister of National Defence should be very strong, he should have a triple metal armour around his breast, to be able to resist the advice of his former president. Pretty tough. I object the more to it because the same man, the Minister of National Defence, is, according to an old order in council, the perpetual acting Minister of Finance, replacing the present Minister of Finance the moment he leaves the limits of the city of Ottawa. That is another reason why I object to it. I find that the Minister of National Defence in his capacity as perpetual acting Minister of Finance has as his personal adviser the president of the bank which is just an agency of an English bank of which Melchett of nickel fame is a director, and he should never sit on that board.
This is one reason, but I have other reasons as well. I will go farther than I did at first because I have been called to order. Precision is wanted and I will give it. I object to the Minister of Munitions and Supply being on that board, and I do so for a very good reason. He has rendered shapeless accounts of his department and now he is rendering none. As a member of the House of Commons, sir, you have no doubt received, as others have done, these shapeless records of contracts awarded by the Department of Munitions and Supply. They started in the month of July, 1940, to print books. Before that time the records were mimeographed, but from July, 1940, until the fall of 1941, they were published in book form and this is the size of these books: 673 pages; 772; 533; 603; 580; 468; 459; 409 ; 596 ; 723; 828 ; 873. That is a total of 7,517 pages of information which was not worth a piece of paper on which nothing is printed-why? Because he never mentioned the quantum. He said, for instance, that there were contracts with Canada Packers for meat or dressed meat, so much money, but no one knew the quantity sold or the price paid for it, or for lumber or for anything else. The contract was mentioned, but the quantum was not mentioned, so that no one knew what the price was.

I do not know how many individual securities have been purchased, but it has not been the policy of either the South African government or the British government to repatriate the South African securities; it is not a matter of government policy. In this house we are dealing with government policy, not with the actions of individual companies.
Apparently hon. members to my far left wish to have those securities repatriated. I thought they had no use for securities, no use for money or other things, but if that were done we would find the control of some of our greatest assets transferred to the United States, the only market able to handle such a volume of securities. I for one am glad the government have not asked for the repatriation of those securities; I am glad to think these great enterprises are still controlled by Britain and ourselves.
In connection with this bill there is one danger I should like to mention, because I am not sure that it is being adequately emphasized in this house. At the present time we
Mutual Aid Bill

are confronted with a climacteric in the progress of the war, brought about very largely by the gun beating the armour, and when I say "armour" I use the word in a military sense, meaning armoured vehicles and tanks. In the early days of the war the armour had its way against all opposition. We have now developed our weapons to the extent that the gun has made the tank no longer the prime weapon of attack it was two years ago, except after a break-through. Therefore we have entirely to adjust our methods and procedures of production. This may and no doubt will cause quite a considerable dislocation of industry. Some industries will close; others will open elsewhere. One thing I wish to emphasize strongly is that when the war is over, we must not find ourselves the possessors of only war industries. Some thought should now be given to the * utilization of our war industry, after the war is over. I refer in detail to the aircraft industry. I see by the press that the production of Lancaster bombers at Malton has been discontinued. Possibly that is a wise procedure. I think, however, it is unfortunate, because poor, unhappy Malton has had so many misfortunes during the war that to add one more is rather hard.
I wish the government to make sure that it does not entirely do away with industries such as the aircraft industry. In Canada we probably have the ability to produce plastic aircraft, or craft of the Mosquito type. We have the wood, the raw materials, the ability to produce, and the scientists. In fact, some of the early developers of that type of construction of air frames were found in Canada. I understand some of the earliest experiments were actually done in this country.
After the war-and no one realizes more than I do that the war is not yet won-we shall be met with the desperate problem of turning our industry over to peace-time production. If we are in the manufacture of plastic aircraft, there will be less difficulty, and I would urge that the government maintain that industry as far as possible. I realize that we have to give equal shares, and that we must meet the other united nations in the joint demand. But I hope we shall not find ourselves with an industry which must be completely scrapped after the war is over.
I mention this on account of recent news. It may be conceivable that the internal strife in Europe may cause a debacle in Germany this year. That is conceivably possible. I do not by any means say it will happen, but it is possible, and I say we must take all eventualities, or as many as possible, into account. That is what I have to say respecting aircraft.

To-day we are building ships. Any ship to-day is a valuable ship. Any ship we can build is a vital ship. Any bottom which will cross the ocean is essential. But at the end of the war we shall find ourselves in the position-and here again I qualify my remarks by what I said before-of competing with shipbuilding firms like John Brown, Swan Hunter, and Harland and Wolf, any of whom can produce ships which will be far more efficient, and which will be better and cheaper carriers than anything we could produce. We shall also be up against the Scandinavian countries, whose operation of ships will be much cheaper than ours. We came across that problem at the end of the last war, and therefore I would) caution the country not to build too great hopes on a great merchant marine in Canada.
With regard to this billion dollars I say that, no matter how it is paid, no matter what machinery is put into operation to produce this fund, it is little enough that we can do to send our allies this equipment. We have been saved by others. We are a very poor example, both to them and to ourselves, if we do not gladly give them the tools they still want.

Just a word in reply to what was said by the hon. member for York. West. His remarks were in two sections. First he praised the views expressed by the hon. lady member for North Battleford, and then he referred to Canadians, without mentioning names, who seemed to want an enemy victory. I challenge him to name anyone in this house who is wishing a victory by the enemy. The county which I represent has done its duty. It is a rural constituency, and about 2,500 boys have enlisted in the three branches of the armed services. That is a satisfactory result. I am receiving letters from these soldiers at all times, and I try to look after their welfare. I try to see to it that they receive proper medical care, and at times I try to obtain transfers for boys who speak only French and who may be in camps where nobody else speaks that language. I try to help their dependents. I take advantage of every opportunity to do something for these boys or their dependents. I am delighted to do this, and I am sure that all members from Quebec are doing the same.
I remember last year when I was advocating the case of the farmer another member from Toronto said that I was close to Hitler because I was taking this attitude, because I wanted the farmer to stay on the farm to produce the food needed by the army as well as by the civilian population. At that time we were ahead of selective service. Whatever may be said against any member from Quebec will not make us forget the hon. gentleman's defence of the selfish financial interests who control Falconbridge Nickel. I do not need to name the directors of this company, but I have it here in the Annual Financial Review, Canadian edition. He has no right to cast aspersions upon anyone and then defend the selfish financial interests, this small group in Toronto which has a nickel plant in Norway, now occupied territory. They speak about the sacrifices they are making, but my farmers are making much greater .sacrifices when their sons are in the army defending this country and facing the possibility of being killed by ammunition made from the nickel that comes from Norway. I would not change positions with the hon. member for York West. I am always ready to defend my people, while he is defending these selfish interests. It is the international makers of armaments, the armaments trusts, who started this war.
We are doing our duty, and yet we are misrepresented by the ho'n. member. He may have friends among the directors of this company; that is his business, but I contend that the soldier in the field who comes from Temiscouata or from any other county deserves more from the country than a defence of the interests with a factory in Norway who are glad that Hitler did not destroy it and that it is now doing quite well.

There are a few observations
I should like to make relative to section 4. I have not taken the opportunity prior to this time to give expression to my feeling with respect to the general principle of the bill, namely, that I wholeheartedly approve

that principle. We in this group have, over a period of years, consistently advocated that we should at all times maintain an optimum level of production in the country and that we should lay particular stress upon maximum distribution within the country. That principle must, of course, be modified in a certain degree when we are confronted with war conditions. We readily appreciate that certain shortages inevitably arise, particularly as they concern consumer goods. That principle of optimum production plus maximum distribution does not apply only to the internal economy of this country, but more particularly in war time it is a condition which applies to the allied nations as a whole. We believe that it is the duty of Canada and Canadians, far removed as we are from the threat of invasion, and-if I may use the expression-from, actual invasion, to enhance our production not only of foodstuffs but also of war materials to the greatest possible degree, and that we should adopt as our main policy one which makes it possible- to export our surpluses, whether they be of foodstuffs or of war materials, to our allies.
The question sometimes arises in the minds of some people, is it proper to expect Canada .to stimulate its production to the highest possible degree and to give, if necessary, the surpluses to the peoples of other countries? Well, I say, if Canada is removed from invasion or the threat of invasion, we should thank God for that and we should thank Him that we have the opportunity of providing surpluses which we can give, if necessary, to those engaged wuth us in this conflict. It is not a question in my mind as to whether Canada may be doing more than some other country. We all have everything at stake in the conflict, and if we can give twice as much as another country, I say once again we ought to thank the Almighty for that privilege.
Need should be the determining factor in shaping our policy; that is, the need of another country, not that country's ability to pay. If China, which has never been very far removed from the famine line, requires our surplus commodities, we should not for one moment stop to consider whether China can pay. The same applies to Russia and to any of our allies. I am afraid that we have allowed-and I see it in section 4 of this bill-the question of the need to escape us, because in that section I notice the word "exchange". I visualize exactly that thing against which the minister stormed last week: for example, "cash on the barrelhead", as he called it. I shall come to that in a few minutes.
I think it is to the credit of the people of Canada that we have been able to achieve

Mutual Aid Bill
the things we have achieved since the outbreak of war. I know we have expanded our production of foodstuffs far beyond the imaginations of most of our people-at least, of their imaginations prior to the outbreak of war. Probably our production of war supplies and the tools of war has also expanded much beyond we believed was possible at the time war broke out. These things are definitely to our credit. On the basis of our productive capacity as realized since the outbreak of war, we have undertaken not only to support a much larger industrial population than we have ever supported before; we have undertaken to support, both with foodstuffs and the tools of war,. the largest army, navy and air force we have ever had. On top of that we have made certain definite commitments abroad. Those commitments have not only to do with the countries actually engaged in the prosecution of the war at the present time; they are also commitments and promises to the subjugated peoples of Europe, whom we have promised something better than the nazis are now giving them, after we have released them from this nazi tyranny. I have in mind, for example, Greece, where they tell us that half a million people starved last year. I have in mind a recent statement to the effect that the Greeks face extermination on account of food scarcity. We have promised those people assistance the minute we can release them; in fact, certain assistance, I understand, is going to them now through the Red Cross. We have promised them food, and we must be prepared to keep that promise. The same applies to all the other subjugated countries of Europe, because, if we cannot keep our promise to them when the war is over, tragedy will come upon the world.
I mention these facts because I believe we should be directing every energy in Canada toward the greater production of, more especially, foodstuffs. We all recognize that Germany did not collapse during the last war as a result of the military difficulties which confronted her, but she tried to devote too large a part of her energy to the actual production of military machines and so forth. Germany adopted an entirely different policy during this war. Germany taught her people over a period of years to do with less. Germany undertook the development of synthetic products to a greater degree probably .than most countries; and not only that, but she laid cleverly designed plans to subjugate rich agricultural areas in order to be guaranteed the foodstuffs essential for total war.

Mutual Aid Bill
we can take care of the situation. I will refrain from transgressing the rules of the house if it is believed that that is what I have been doing. But I still have one or two matters that I should like to mention which I am satisfied are within the rules.
Let me refer to section 4 of this bill wherein it is stated that this Mutual Aid board shall be authorized to deliver certain goods to the allied nations, transfer title to such goods, contribute them or make them available; and then we come to the word "exchange." My conception of the Mutual Aid bill is that we were preparing to make a gift to our allies; the term has been used by many hon. members. Yet throughout, the discussion thus far we have heard about demanding certain goods in return, trading some of our goods given under this appropriation for certain goods which the countries that receive our goods may be able to send back. We also discussed the possible necessity of having much of our own machinery returned, following the cessation of hostilities, if it is not worn out. I do not believe I can be accused of being in a much different position from that of others when I say I have become confused. Speaking on the resolution-I trust I am in order in referring to what the minister said when we were dealing with the resolution that preceded this bill-the minister was referring to a contention of the hon. member for Acadia that we should take steps toward repatriating Canadian securities held in England. I know that is not going to be done, and I do not intend to pursue that point farther, but the minister at that time lashed out with a degree of enthusiasm bordering almost on frenzy when he said, as reported at page 2456 of Hansard:
I say very solemnly that with the United States pursuing the policy it is, and with Great Britain pursuing the policy it is, for us to revert to a cash-on-the-barrel-head policy would be unthinkable; it would be indefensible; it *would be intolerable.
I lay emphasis on those three words, "unthinkable", "indefensible" and "intolerable". Maybe I do not know what the minister means when he uses the term "cash on the barrel-head". I take it he means either that they will demand immediate payment or get the assurance that similar goods will be returned at a later date, or even that those goods which do not wear out, that formerly helonged to us, will be returned. Does the minister include that in his definition of "cash on the barrel-head"? If not, I do not know what he means.

When we use the term "cash" with respect to imports and exports I think the minister is perfectly clear what that means. Let us not convey the impression that when we send goods to England, England immediately ships back a 'barrelful of money or anything of that kind. We understand that trade is carried on to a large extent through the exchange of goods. Therefore I contend that when we export commodities to England and accept commodities in return, that certainly is not a gift; and it does come within any reasonable definition of cash on the barrel-head. When the minister writes his dictionary he may put a different meaning on that expression. In order to keep the minister perfectly straight as far as his definitions are concerned, I am going to move that the word "exchange" be deleted. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Battle River:
That paragraph 1 of section 4 be amended by striking out the word "exchange" in line three of said paragraph.
I do so in order to eliminate some of the confusion which has apparently arisen, so that in the debate that follows we may have a clear-cut picture as to what part of the billion dollars will be a gift and what part we are to accept payment for. I believed from the beginning that it was to be a gift of goods to our allies; I sincerely trust that I am not wrong in that understanding.

I understand that the technique will be somewhat different under this bill from what it was last year when the entire amount was going to Great Britain.
A number of questions arise in my mind. The first is, on what basis will this sum be allocated as between different united nations? Will it be determined by the board, or will it be determined in consultation with the united nations board at Washington? Will the grand strategy of the united nations be the determining factor rather than this board?
The second question I have in mind is this. In the spending of this thousand million dollars, how will it be allocated as between different kinds of goods? For instance, will an amount be set for these governments; will they come in and place their orders for commodities, with the understanding that the . Canadian government will simply meet the financial obligations which they have incurred up to a certain amount, or will this board determine what goods they are prepared to turn over and actually purchase the goods and turn them over? Then, arising out of that question, if this procedure is followed, how will these arrangements be brought about? For instance, will the British or Chinese or Russian government place orders with factories and have that obligation met by this board, or will the Canadian government place the order, buy the goods and turn them over? In the case of agricultural products, for instance, will these products be bought by the Canadian government, or will the government of the other nation concerned make the deal, buy the commodity and then have this board simply foot the bill up to an amount which has been agreed upon? I wonder if the minister could just outline something of the technique that has been or will be followed.

No, nothing has been done under this. Up to date we have been able to finance by other methods: with the money the United Kingdom obtained as the purchase price of the plants, and in the other ways I have mentioned in the various statements I have made in the house. This has made it unnecessary for any transactions to take place under this bill; as a matter of fact they could not take place under this bill.
With regard to the first question asked by the hon. member for Weyburn, as to how the supplies will be allocated among the various united nations who receive them, the reply is that they will be allocated by this board. The question then arises as to whether the programme of this board will conflict in any way with the munitions assignment boards which are sitting in Washington and London. In order to prevent it from conflicting it will be necessary to keep in very close touch with those boards and see that there is a harmonious programme, but I will not say it will be a programme determined by the munitions assignment boards, because this board will have the determining voice as to how this allocation is made. It will have to be a rational allocation, having in mind the disposition of goods that is being made by the assignment boards..

Mutual Aid Bill
The second question was as to how the billion dollars will be allocated as between the various commodities described in or covered by this bill. That will have to be worked out, and I cannot say in advance what will be done in that connection. Some commodities produced in the Dominion of Canada will be sold in the ordinary course, I suppose, through private transactions. They would not come under this bill at all. I presume some commodities will be sold by governmental agencies, because there will have to be quite a good deal of selling. If our trade keeps up to its accustomed level, we shall export to the united nations much more than a billion dollars worth of goods. Part of those goods will, of course, be paid for by these nations from the proceeds of their exports to us, the services they render to us, and so on. So that there will be a certain volume of transactions taking place other than under the provisions of this legislation. Whether those transactions or sales will have to be based upon or related to the contributions made under this measure is a matter that will have to be worked out. I think the whole picture will have to be kept before the Mutual Aid board, but farther than that I do not think I can map out anything definitely. One cannot say what nations will pay and what nations will not pay; that any nation will be expected to pay in the same proportion as any other nation, because something will depend upon the volume of their dollar resources. Something will depend upon their capacity to do something for us in some way or another, which they may very reasonably be expected to do. They may have some product of which we are in need and which they might be very willing to let us have, or there might be some service they could render for us. That is about the best picture I can present at the moment.

I should like to ask a question of the minister in respect of agricultural products, and the method whereby allocation will be made harmoniously among the nations requiring assistance. I was rather surprised the other day, upon reading the speech of the secretary of agriculture in the United States, to find just how great a place is occupied by agricultural products under the lend-lease arrangements. Under the system of lend-lease in effect in the United States a great quantity of agricultural products has been delivered to Great Britain. But the amazing part of the situation is that in contra-lend-lease Great Britain has given the United States a great deal of agricultural products.
For the purpose of showing the nature of the contribution made by Great Britain, let me point out that within the last year Britain has supplied United States citizens in Great Britain with 101,000,000 pounds of flour, over
41,000,000 pounds of potatoes, 50,000,000 pounds of butter, and so on. Agricultural products have played a large part in lend-lease arrangements. Yet there is a combined production board in Washington, and a combined munitions distribution board, on which Canada has representatives. But on the combined food board we are not- represented. I suggest to the minister that Canada should be represented, now that she is embarking upon a system of lend-lease and Mutual Aid which will necessarily come in conflict with the distribution being made by the United States. In order properly to equalize and determine the proper shares and proper needs of the various united nations, we should have a place upon the combined food allocaton board in Washington.

The matter of representation on boards is one of high policy concerning which I should not like to make any statement.

Then he went on to point out the difficulties. I cannot understand how a board consisting of ministers of the crown in Canada can administer fairly and properly, according to the needs of the nations requiring assistance, the distribution of farm products and the like, unless we have membership upon that board. The position of affairs under this measure will be that the United States of America and the other united nations will make distribution, according to the needs of nations, as determined by the joint board; and Canada will operate independently of a central, unified control.
I suggest to the minister that for Canada to have a place upon the combined food allocation board in Washington is the only way in which the measure can be administered, provided it is intended to allocate a fair and proper proportion of this billion dollars to the distribution of agricultural products.
I am not going to discuss the other phase of the matter which I dealt with the other day, namely, that having to do with trade agreements which might be entered into under the provisions of this section. I have dealt with that matter at length, and I shall not deal with it again, more than to point out that the minister admitted to-day that under section 4 it would be possible for the Mutual Aid board of Canada to ask, in return for the delivery, contribution, or making available of war supplies to any of the united nations, for the execution of a trade agreement with that united nation. When I asked him to give an assurance that that would not be done, the answer was that he could not give such assurance.
That being so, and wishing in no way to interfere with the right of Mutual Aid board to do what is necessary in order to assure a proper and fair distribution of the assistance which Canada will give under this measure, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle:
That section 4 be amended by adding to subsection 2 the following words:
"Provided, however, that any reciprocal trade or tariff agreement made in pursuance of this subsection to be binding upon Canada must be given the approval of parliament within six months after the signing of such agreement".
I place the amendment before the committee, not with a view to controlling the actions and the discretion of the Mutual Aid board now being set up, but with a view to ensuring that parliament and the representatives of the people shall have an opportunity, within a period of six months, of ascertaining what trade arrangements have been entered into. Otherwise the position of affairs is this, that having regard to the provisions of section 8 of the bill, the government or the Mutual Aid board might enter into a trade agreement which would not become known to parliament or the people until after the termination of the war.
I ask thp minister whether, having regard to his frank assurance that there is no suggestion or intention on the part of the Mutual Aid board or the government to exact or ask for trade agreements in return for assistance in the cause of international defence among the united nations, this amendment might be accepted by the government.

A few minutes ago I was trying to get some information from the minister with regard to the procedure which would be followed by the board in carrying out its functions under section 4. There are just two points I wish to make. I appreciate that we cannot be told the allocation of the materials, what materials will be given to any particular nation, but it seems to me that it should be possible to outline more clearly the procedure that will be followed and the underlying factors that will determine the decisions which will be made by this board. The preamble states that these materials are to be made available according to strategic needs and in such manner as will contribute most effectively to the winning of the war. I am wondering just how these strategic needs will be made known. Will China and Russia or other members of the united nations make representations to Canada through the external affairs department or direct to the board, or will they be made through the assignment board?
What about foodstuffs? We have no representatives on the food board in Washington, and I should like to know how the needs of these countries with reference to foodstuffs will be .made known to this board. I am a little afraid that there may not be a proper liaison between this committee, and the general strategy of the united nations. Unless this board knows the general strategy of the united nations and is in contact with those who are guiding the high policy of the united nations, it will not be in a position to make allocations in the most effective manner. I can see -where there would be some liaison in the matter of munitions, because the minister who is to be the chairman of this board is also a member of the priorities board in Washington.

But that is not true of foodstuffs, nor is it true of the munitions board of Great Britain, although the chairman of that board is represented here and there is some liaison.
The other matter I have in mind is in connection with agricultural products. I gathered from what'the minister said that some foodstuffs will be bought by government agencies and disposed of to the united nations, while other foodstuffs will be bought by the united nations through their own representatives or purchased through the usual channels of trade. Even though we are actually giving them these materials, the fact remains that the more buyers there are on the market the greater will be the tendency to keep down prices where prices are not pegged. It seems to me that this is a fairly good argument for the position we have taken all along, that we ought to have commodity boards set up by the government, taking delivery of these commodities at a price to be determined by the government in consultation with the organized producers, and then these commodity boards either selling or making available through this legislation these commodities to the united nations. It would prevent a number of buyers from coming in, through different government agencies and other channels, competing on the market and naturally affecting the price. There would be more satisfactory handling if these commodities were dealt with through a commodity board.

You might have government agencies; you have, for example, in wheat at this very time. You have the wheat board offering one price; you have buyers coming on the market and offering another price. You have, for instance, the Americans with a much higher price for cereal grains, with the result that we have had to take steps, either to prevent the export of these cereal grains, or to require would-be sellers to have permits to export them. The farmer gets one price if he sells to the wheat board, another price when he is selling on the open Winnipeg market, and another price if it is possible for him to get his commodities across the line. I do not think that is quite good enough. What I want the minister to do is to give as much detail as possible as to what the government propose to do with the billion dollars.
I want hon. members who object to the principle of the gift to know that, in all these international operations, the traffic is not all one way. I think it will be a matter of very great surprise to hon. members to know what Britain has done for the United States under lease-lend. I hold in my hand an article taken from the Atlantic Monthly of a recent issue, and it is astonishing what Britain has done for the United States under lease-lend.
